title_en: Why your AirPods keep disconnecting without warning: These settings can fix it
title_fa: Why your AirPods keep disconnecting without warning: These settings can fix it
excerpt_en: Handy features of your AirPods can be overzealous, leading to disconnections and unwanted device swapping.
excerpt_fa: Handy features of your AirPods can be overzealous, leading to disconnections and unwanted device swapping.
content_en:
Why your AirPods keep disconnecting without warning: These settings can fix it
Before blaming Bluetooth, check where your AirPods are getting their orders from.
If your AirPods keep disconnecting, it's doubtful the AirPods themselves are broken, though that's always a possibility. The best course of action is a process of elimination, starting with checking automatic switching. This feature is available on all AirPods Pro and AirPods Max models, plus AirPods 2 or later.
Let's say you have your iPhone, an iPad and a Mac. If you use your AirPods on all three, or have in the past, those bothersome disconnections may not be disconnections at all, but rather the AirPods trying to bounce back and forth among all three devices. It's aggravating, but you need to make changes on all three to put a stop to it.
The setting you want is called Connect to this iPhone/iPad/Mac. First, put your AirPods in your ears. On iPhone or iPad, you should see your AirPods appear near the top of the Settings app. There, select your AirPods > Audio & Routing > Connect to this iPhone/iPad and choose When Last Connected to This iPhone/iPad.
Alternatively, or in System Settings on a Mac, open Settings > Bluetooth and select the little i in a circle next to your AirPods. If the AirPods aren't currently connected, choose Connect to This [Device] > When Last Connected to This [Device]. If they are connected, open the same Audio & Routing menu first.
If you mostly use your AirPods with one device, leave this setting on Automatic there and switch it to When Last Connected on your other Apple devices. That way, your AirPods will automatically connect to your most-used device when you put them in, but won't connect to your other devices unless you manually choose to use them. This won't fix every connection problem, but it will correct a common issue with using AirPods across multiple Apple devices.
You can also fully remove your AirPods using the Forget This Device option in the Bluetooth menu on any devices you never use them with.
Automatic Ear Detection can interrupt playback
The next time your AirPods disconnect, check to make sure they've actually disconnected by looking in the Bluetooth menu. AirPods have a feature called Automatic Ear Detection, which is enabled by default. It does what its name implies: detects when you remove your earbuds and automatically halts playback. It's a handy feature when you need to pull a bud out to hear what someone is saying, but if the sensor is misbehaving, it will interrupt your music for seemingly no reason.
Before you turn this off, it's worth making sure your AirPods are fitting properly. With your AirPods in your ears, go to the same AirPods menu mentioned above and hit Ear Tip Fit Test in the list. This will run a quick check to see if your buds have a good seal; if the tips you're using are the wrong size for your ears, or dirty, they're more likely to slip out.
Clean your AirPods and consider upgrading your earbud tips so they stay in and comfortable for long periods. It's important to clean the case too, as bits of earwax or trapped lint can block the electrical contact points and prevent one or both of your AirPods from charging. Special troubleshooting applies if only one of your AirPods isn't working.
In case this doesn't help or you want to disable the feature anyway, put your AirPods in and go back to Settings > AirPods > Audio & Routing, then disable Automatic Ear Detection. The process is the same on a Mac or an iPad. Now that it's off, check to see if the disconnections continue. If they do, check the audio of a download versus a stream; if problems only happen on the latter, network issues are causing your audio to stutter. And if you spend a lot of time close to a microwave, many other Bluetooth devices or heavy Wi-Fi activity, interference could be causing your AirPods to misbehave.
Having Siri turned on can interrupt playback if the assistant kicks in for whatever reason. You can eliminate that by jumping into Settings > Siri > Requests and setting the top option to Off, though this turns Siri off for your entire device as there's no toggle for the AirPods alone.
My AirPods are disconnecting from my Mac. What can I do?
Start by eliminating the automatic switching feature on your other devices, as explained above. It's a pain because it's convenient to let your AirPods bounce to whatever device you're currently using. But when another device turns on, it becomes a battle between which one started playing audio most recently. If you typically move from device to device but don't always close the last one, it's best to keep Automatically selected on your primary and When Last Connected to on all the others.
Also, open Control Center at the top-right of your Mac's screen. Select Sound and confirm the output is set to your AirPods. Make sure you quit any apps that are vying for control of your AirPods. Check if your Mac is up to date, and you can let your AirPods run any pending firmware updates as well. To do this, connect the case to power and put both earbuds inside, closing the lid afterward. Leave them within Bluetooth range of your Wi-Fi-connected Mac, iPhone or iPad for at least 30 minutes.
If the connection failures continue to happen, unpair your AirPods from your Mac, restart the Mac and pair the AirPods again. As a last resort, you may have to do a full reset on your AirPods. The sequence depends on the model, so follow Apple's AirPods reset guidance.

excerpt_fa: After hackers stole a shocking $6.3 billion from Binance customers in a record-breaking crypto heist, the company's CEO says that 90 percent of the funds have been replaced, and the company plans to cover the remaining 10 percent as well. Binance is covering the stolen funds...
content_en:
After hackers stole a shocking $6.3 billion from Binance customers in a record-breaking crypto heist, the company’s CEO says that 90 percent of the funds have been replaced, and the company plans to cover the remaining 10 percent as well. Binance is covering the stolen funds directly, and the remaining 10 percent consists of “less liquid” tokens, which the company says may take longer to acquire.
Binance CEO says 90 percent of stolen assets have been ‘replenished’
Most of the $6.3 billion in crypto stolen from Binance users has been restored.
Most of the $6.3 billion in crypto stolen from Binance users has been restored.
The company also said in a post on X that, while withdrawals remain paused, they’re on track to be enabled on Sunday.
Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions.
Our next milestone in focus is resuming the withdrawal services for users. We remain on track to reopen withdrawals within our previously stated timeframe (on Sunday, 2026-11-01) and will provide a further update as soon as details are confirmed.

title_en: How to use Claude Duet when it rolls out to you
title_fa: How to use Claude Duet when it rolls out to you
excerpt_en: For now, you'll need to first join a waitlist.
excerpt_fa: For now, you'll need to first join a waitlist.
content_en:
How to use Claude Duet when it rolls out to you
For now, you'll need to first join a waitlist.
On October 21, following SpaceXSI, Meta and OpenAI, Anthropic became the latest AI lab to release a personal agent. Like its competitors, the company is billing Claude Duet as an always-on AI agent that can proactively complete tasks for you, even when you're away from your phone or computer. Duet runs on its own virtual machine, with access to a dedicated browser it can use to surf the web and complete jobs. It can also use any apps you've connected to your Claude account. If you're curious about Claude Duet, here's what you need to know about availability and how much it will cost you to run the agent.
How to join the Claude Duet waiting list
As of the writing of this article, Duet is currently in preview, with availability limited to Claude Pro and Max subscribers in the US. What's more, you'll need to join a waitlist before you can start using the agent. You can find that waitlist on Anthropic's website. The company asks you to enter your name, company and email address. You'll also need to indicate the type of phone you use, be it an Android or iPhone, and write a short description of the type of work you intend to hand off to Claude. Anthropic asks you to share what device you use because it offers a standalone Claude Duet app on Android and iOS.
What Anthropic plans include Claude Duet?
While things may change, Anthropic says it will include Duet as a perk of its $20 per month Pro plan and up. Notably, that differs from OpenAI's Dot agents, which you can currently only get by paying for one of the company's own Pro plans. That tier starts at $100, with OpenAI recently adding a $500 per month option. Anthropic isn't making Claude Duet available to Team and Enterprise customers just yet.
During the preview, Anthropic says Duet will share usage with all your other Claude apps, including Code and Cowork. I haven't had a chance to use it yet, so I can't speak to whether Duet is actually useable with a Pro plan, but Anthropic has said it designed the agent to check your connected accounts every few hours, "because checking nonstop would use up your plan's limits much faster." Part of the reason the company is previewing Duet before rolling it out more widely is so that it can collect feedback on how often it messages users.
What can you do with Claude Duet?
As I mentioned, Anthropic is advertising Duet as a proactive personal agent. Each day, it can generate a short briefing with a list of action items based on the apps you've connected to your Claude account. You can also delegate a variety of tasks to Claude Duet. For instance, you can ask it to schedule meetings for you, create forecasts, build web apps and more. For example, a business owner might task Duet with generating a weekly sales and cashflow dashboard, while a scientist could ask their agent to flag research papers related to their area of study as they're published.
"The Claude app waits for you to open a chat, and you work on something alongside Claude. Claude Duet comes to you," Anthropic says. "It tells you what needs your attention each morning, takes tasks you hand it by message, and reaches out when one is done or needs your approval."
Duet's proactivity is built on the data in your Claude account, including information the chatbot has written to its memory and any apps you've connected to your Anthropic account. For that reason, how useful you might find Duet will depend a lot on how much of your digital life you're willing to share with Anthropic. For some, the privacy tradeoff is not going to be worth it.

title_en: 4 drawbacks you should know before buying a PlayStation 5
title_fa: 4 drawbacks you should know before buying a PlayStation 5
excerpt_en: The PS5 isn't as good of a buy today as it was early in its life, so you should be aware of the drawbacks in this awkward console generation.
excerpt_fa: The PS5 isn't as good of a buy today as it was early in its life, so you should be aware of the drawbacks in this awkward console generation.
content_en:
4 drawbacks you should know before buying a PlayStation 5
Now isn't the best time to buy a PS5, so know what you're in for first.
There's arguably never been a worse time to be a PlayStation fan or buy a PS5, with systems more than half a decade old costing more now than they did at release. RAMageddon is screwing tech fans worldwide, and Sony seems dead-set on burning the goodwill it's built up. We're at a particularly bad point to invest in a game console.
While both the PS5 and upgraded PS5 Pro are great systems, neither represents decent value for money right now — especially when we don't have any idea when a PlayStation 6 is going to launch.
PlayStation's discless future is anti-consumer
Sony won't put games on discs starting in 2028, which means when the PS6 eventually comes out, it won't support physical games. Sony is seemingly doubling down on killing disc-based media going forward, per FlatpanelsHD's reporting that the UBP-X700/K will be the last 4K Blu-ray player the company manufactures.
So as of 2028, Sony will end the PlayStation's legacy as a true media hub. That's frustrating given how many past consoles made strides in this area. The PS2's DVD playback was a huge part of its enormous popularity, while the PS3 was one of the most affordable Blu-ray players of its time. I stood in line to buy a PS2 on November 24, 2000 not just to play EA's snowboarding classic SSX, but also because that system let me play my brand-new DVD copy of Jurassic Park for the first time. Discovering chapter skip and DVD extras on what's still my favorite film of all time was an awesome moment.
That will all be gone soon. GTA VI will just be a code in a box if you buy the "physical" version, for example. Soon, there won't be an option to loan games to friends or take advantage of in-store sales.
I take a share of the blame for the switch to digital. During this generation, the only PS5 games I've bought on disc, out of my 36-title PS5 library, are Demon's Souls, Marvel's Spider-Man 2, God of War Ragnarök and Saros. That means I've purchased a mere 11 percent of my PlayStation 5 games physically over the six years I've owned the console, which feels wrong as a self-proclaimed defender of physical media.
No version of the PS5 is cheap
Not only are the two launch models, supercharged Pro and svelte PS5 Slim not cheap, all four machines are significantly more expensive than when they first launched. In past generations, consoles have gotten cheaper the longer they're on the market. But in the era of extreme RAM shortages, where Sony is forced to hike up hardware costs because memory and SSD prices have never been more expensive, gamers' wallets are being hit hard.
When the original disc drive PlayStation 5 and cheaper Digital Edition launched in North America on November 12, 2020, their respective $499 and $399 price tags were pretty reasonable — especially considering the PS4's $400 launch price and the PS3's infamous $599 from 14 years prior.
Want to pick up either the disc drive PS5 or discless version now? It will cost you $649 for the disc-equipped system, or $599 if you don't care about physical games. That means the PS5 is now 30 percent (disc) and 50 percent (digital) more expensive than in 2020. Ouch. At least the disc model has 1TB of storage compared to 825GB at launch, though the Digital Slim has dropped to the lower storage amount again.
Not surprisingly, the PS5 Pro has seen its own increases. When the beefed-up console launched in Nov 7 2024, it cost $699. Now, it will put a massive $899 dent in your bank balance — if you can find one. We're in the middle of a PS5 Pro shortage because people are desperate for a mythic GTA VI 60 fps performance mode that neither Rockstar or Sony have confirmed ahead of launch. Still, that hasn't stopped cheeky third-party Amazon sellers from trying to charge $1,449 for a used PS5 Pro. But hey, at least the optional Slim/Pro disc drive still costs the same $79 as it did upon the upgraded console's arrival.
The PS5 Pro is powerful, but its CPU holds it back
The PlayStation 5 Pro is the most powerful video game console of all time. Yet as impressive as the Pro's specs are, it can't hold a candle to the most powerful gaming PCs. Even though it packs considerably more graphical grunt under the hood than the standard PS5, one key component somewhat holds back its full potential.
On the CPU front, the PS5 Pro's processor upgrade over the standard console is modest. Both consoles use AMD Zen 2 eight core/16 thread processors. The Pro upgrade is that its chip is clocked at 3.85GHz vs. the standard PS5's 3.5GHz clock. In real-world terms, that's just a 10 percent upgrade; such a measly bump is likely why we're not seeing 90 fps modes in CPU-intensive PS5 titles like Cyberpunk 2077 and Dragon's Dogma 2 on the Pro.
From a GPU standpoint, the PS5 Pro's specs look a lot more robust next to the vanilla PS5. The Pro's graphical solution outputs 16.7 TFLOPS of GPU compute power, compared to the base PlayStation 5's (still respectable) 10.3 FLOPS. That's a polygon-pushing 45 percent boost. The number of GPU compute units is also heavily in favor of the Pro, with the newer system having a 60-36 advantage over the standard PS5.
PSSR 2.0 upscaling tech also makes Resident Evil Requiem and Saros look incredible on the Pro. Yet with Sony bringing AI upscaling to the base PS5 — in the form of Quick Spectral Super Resolution or "QSSR" — the gap between the two consoles has become thinner.
The PS5 is arguably the ugliest console Sony has ever made
A few friends of mine who hadn't gamed since the PS2 era all bought PS5s during the pandemic, but none of them proudly show off their OG launch model. I'm sure this is in no small part due to their significant others who all see Sony's latest console for what it is: an eyesore. content_fa:
4 drawbacks you should know before buying a PlayStation 5
Now isn't the best time to buy a PS5, so know what you're in for first.
There's arguably never been a worse time to be a PlayStation fan or buy a PS5, with systems more than half a decade old costing more now than they did at release. RAMageddon is screwing tech fans worldwide, and Sony seems dead-set on burning the goodwill it's built up. We're at a particularly bad point to invest in a game console.
While both the PS5 and upgraded PS5 Pro are great systems, neither represents decent value for money right now — especially when we don't have any idea when a PlayStation 6 is going to launch.
PlayStation's discless future is anti-consumer
Sony won't put games on discs starting in 2028, which means when the PS6 eventually comes out, it won't support physical games. Sony is seemingly doubling down on killing disc-based media going forward, per FlatpanelsHD's reporting that the UBP-X700/K will be the last 4K Blu-ray player the company manufactures.
So as of 2028, Sony will end the PlayStation's legacy as a true media hub. That's frustrating given how many past consoles made strides in this area. The PS2's DVD playback was a huge part of its enormous popularity, while the PS3 was one of the most affordable Blu-ray players of its time. I stood in line to buy a PS2 on November 24, 2000 not just to play EA's snowboarding classic SSX, but also because that system let me play my brand-new DVD copy of Jurassic Park for the first time. Discovering chapter skip and DVD extras on what's still my favorite film of all time was an awesome moment.
That will all be gone soon. GTA VI will just be a code in a box if you buy the "physical" version, for example. Soon, there won't be an option to loan games to friends or take advantage of in-store sales.
I take a share of the blame for the switch to digital. During this generation, the only PS5 games I've bought on disc, out of my 36-title PS5 library, are Demon's Souls, Marvel's Spider-Man 2, God of War Ragnarök and Saros. But in the era of extreme RAM shortages, where Sony is forced to hike up hardware costs because memory and SSD prices have never been more expensive, gamers' wallets are being hit hard.

That means the PS5 is now 30 percent (disc) and 50 percent (digital) more expensive than in 2020. Ouch. Now, it will put a massive $899 dent in your bank balance — if you can find one. Still, that hasn't stopped cheeky third-party Amazon sellers from trying to charge $1,449 for a used PS5 Pro. But hey, at least the optional Slim/Pro disc drive still costs the same $79 as it did upon the upgraded console's arrival.
The PS5 Pro is powerful, but its CPU holds it back
The PlayStation 5 Pro is the most powerful video game console of all time. Yet as impressive as the Pro's specs are, it can't hold a candle to the most powerful gaming PCs. Even though it packs considerably more graphical grunt under the hood than the standard PS5, one key component somewhat holds back its full potential.
On the CPU front, the PS5 Pro's processor upgrade over the standard console is modest. Both consoles use AMD Zen 2 eight core/16 thread processors. The Pro upgrade is that its chip is clocked at 3.85GHz vs. the standard PS5's 3.5GHz clock. In real-world terms, that's just a 10 percent upgrade; such a measly bump is likely why we're not seeing 90 fps modes in CPU-intensive PS5 titles like Cyberpunk 2077 and Dragon's Dogma 2 on the Pro.

The Pro's graphical solution outputs 16.7 TFLOPS of GPU compute power, compared to the base PlayStation 5's (still respectable) 10.3 FLOPS. That's a polygon-pushing 45 percent boost. The number of GPU compute units is also heavily in favor of the Pro, with the newer system having a 60-36 advantage over the standard PS5.
PSSR 2.0 upscaling tech also makes Resident Evil Requiem and Saros look incredible on the Pro. Yet with Sony bringing AI upscaling to the base PS5 — in the form of Quick Spectral Super Resolution or "QSSR" — the gap between the two consoles has become thinner.

content_en:
This morning, Nintendo announced that tomorrow, November 1st, would be the first annual Pikmin Day. As part of the short Pikmin Day Direct, Shigeru Miyamoto shared new info about Pikmin 4 for the Switch 2, as well as an update for the mobile app Pikmin Bloom, and announced the Hello! Pikmin series of shorts.
Happy Pikmin Day Eve
Nintendo is celebrating the first annual Pikmin Day by debuting a new series of short films.
Nintendo is celebrating the first annual Pikmin Day by debuting a new series of short films.
Players will be able to use the Switch 2’s built-in microphone to issue voice commands to Oatchi, the space dog. Pikmin 4 will also have a Dandori Academy mode that will test players’ skills in specific challenges. There will be limited tests on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, complete with leaderboards where players can compare stats. Pikmin Bloom will be getting a new feature called Secret Caves, where players can win treasure by battling enemies and exploring said caves.
Lastly, Miyamoto showed the first installment of a new series of shorts called Hello! Pikmin. A second episode will premiere tomorrow, with a third later in November. The series will then debut one short per month starting in December. The shorts build on the success of Close to You, a Pikmin animation released last year.

title_en: Bolt Graphics powers on its first Zeus GPU
title_fa: Bolt Graphics powers on its first Zeus GPU
excerpt_en: Bolt Graphics has been working on its simulation-centric Zeus GPU for a while now and has reached a significant milestone: a successful test run.
excerpt_fa: Bolt Graphics has been working on its simulation-centric Zeus GPU for a while now and has reached a significant milestone: a successful test run.
content_en:
Bolt Graphics powers on its first Zeus GPU
The test chip ran fine but Bolt's Zeus GPU is still a long way from shipping.
Bolt Graphics has powered on the first silicon for its Zeus GPU project, though the card it's building toward isn't expected to reach volume production until 2028. The California-based startup said in mid-October that its 12nm test chip, made by chipmaking giant TSMC, ran without issues when switched on. Bolt also said it had opened an office in Taipei to stay close to its manufacturing partners ahead of production. Two days later, Reuters reported that Bolt was trying to raise about $100 million at a valuation of around $700 million, citing three people familiar with the matter.
The test chip measures 6mm^2 and draws 1.4 watts, compared with the 35 watts used by the FPGA (a reprogrammable chip used for prototyping) that Bolt previously ran its design on. Its main feature is dedicated hardware for electromagnetic simulation, which helps design everything from radar sensors to camera lenses.
Bolt's CEO and founder Darwesh Singh told HPCwire that the chip shows Bolt can run "a highly complex physics algorithm, accelerated in hardware, which no one's done before." However, Bolt hasn't published any performance figures for the test chip, saying only that it beat the company's internal estimates. The Zeus GPU Bolt plans to debut is a completely separate chip that'll be made on TSMC's N5P process node. Bolt says it picked the 2020-era N5P process to avoid competing with other chipmakers for already limited wafer supplies.
What is Zeus, exactly?
Bolt's Zeus GPU is built around RISC-V processor cores, which use an open-standard instruction set, paired with Bolt's own path-tracing hardware. Its PCIe cards will combine soldered LPDDR5X memory with the DDR5 SO-DIMM slots you'll usually find in a laptop, letting owners expand the cards up to 384GB of memory. When Bolt announced Zeus in March 2025, it made lofty claims of 10 times the rendering performance of existing GPUs and 300 times the speed in electromagnetic simulation, saying Zeus could deliver up to 10 times the path tracing throughput (i.e., how many light rays a rendering system can process per second) of Nvidia's RTX 5090.
As is usually the case in situations like this, these claims have not been independently tested. Bolt is selling Zeus to studios, engineers and scientists first, with plans to expand into gaming and AI later. That'd put Zeus in the consumer GPU market against Nvidia and AMD. That will be an interesting move, given, as Reuters pointed out, the deep software support a gaming chip needs to run the thousands of games already on sale.
Bolt said back in April that more than 14,000 businesses, devs and individual users had signed up for its early access program, and that it had a product pipeline worth more than $500 million. It did not, however, name any customers. In the same announcement, Bolt also claimed that Zeus would cut compute costs by up to 17 times compared with current hardware.

title_en: These Samsung Galaxy Watches won't be getting the new One UI update
title_fa: These Samsung Galaxy Watches won't be getting the new One UI update
excerpt_en: Samsung has released the latest version of its wearable OS, One UI 9 Watch, and most of its watch lineup will get the update - except these.
excerpt_fa: Samsung has released the latest version of its wearable OS, One UI 9 Watch, and most of its watch lineup will get the update - except these.
content_en:
These Samsung Galaxy Watches won't be getting the new One UI update
The list of Galaxy Watches not getting One UI 9 Watch is mercifully small.
In August, Samsung released the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, which came with its latest One UI 9 Watch operating system. The company has also been releasing beta versions of the OS for the Galaxy Watch 7 and 8 lineups, with the sixth One UI 9 Watch beta update launching in late October for Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic Owners in South Korea. Most previous devices will also eventually get the update, but some are now too old to get the latest OS.
While Samsung has bumped up the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2's software support to five major OS upgrades, their predecessors in the Watch lineup only get four. That might mean it's time for an upgrade if you're rocking an especially old Samsung watch. While the lack of One UI 9 Watch won't affect performance, it does mean your watch won't get bug fixes, new features or security updates. Future app compatibility is another question mark. Thankfully, only a couple of products won't get One UI 9 Watch.
Which Galaxy Watch won't get One UI 9?
The Samsung Galaxy Watch devices that won't receive the One UI 9 Watch update are the Galaxy Watch 4 and the Galaxy Watch 4 Classic. Released in 2021, Samsung's Galaxy Watch 4 lineup has already received four major OS upgrades: One UI Watch 4.5, One UI 5 Watch, One UI 6 Watch and finally One UI 8 Watch. Naturally, this includes limited editions like the Galaxy Watch 4 Golf Edition and the pricey Galaxy Watch 4 Classic Thom Browne Edition. The lineup losing support also marks the end of an era, as the Galaxy Watch 4 heralded the transition from Tizen OS to a custom-skinned Wear OS, Google's smartwatch operating system.
Samsung's Galaxy Watch 5, Galaxy Watch 5 Pro and up will receive One UI 9 Watch by the end of 2026. New features include a refined visual interface, the ability to raise your wrist to activate an AI assistant and health metrics like Daily Cardio Load and a Heart Health Score.
Is it a good time to upgrade your Samsung Galaxy Watch?
If you're still rocking a Galaxy Watch 4 or a Galaxy Watch 4 Classic, it's worth upgrading to a newer device to get the latest OS upgrades. The Galaxy Watch 9 debuted in August and, alongside improved hardware and enhanced features like sleep apnea detection and skin temperature tracking, also promises five years of upgrades. This makes it a good long-term proposition, especially compared to the Pixel Watch 5, which only gets three years of guaranteed updates. And if you absolutely need the physical rotating bezel of the Watch 4 Classic, give the Watch 8 Classic a long, hard look.
Selling, recycling or trading in your legacy Galaxy Watch isn't your only option. You can also repurpose it into a dedicated sleep tracker, smart home dashboard, media remote or just hand it down to someone else. Overall, the One UI 9 Watch update isn't exactly life-changing, but it's a good time to think about that device on your wrist and replace it if it's starting to get long in the tooth.

title_en: How to fix your phone screen when it's unresponsive to touch​
title_fa: How to fix your phone screen when it's unresponsive to touch​
excerpt_en: Few things are more annoying than an unresponsive touchscreen. Before you give up on your phone, here's what to try to get it working again.
excerpt_fa: Few things are more annoying than an unresponsive touchscreen. Before you give up on your phone, here's what to try to get it working again.
content_en:
How to fix your phone screen when it's unresponsive to touch
Most stuck screens have a simple fix.
There are a number of reasons that can make your phone's screen unresponsive to your touch. Sometimes it's a simple thing, like an app freezing. Other times, it's something more serious, like your phone falling when you tried to take it out of your pocket (we've all been there). Regardless of the "why," most times, a simple fix can get your pocket's best friend ready for your next scrolling session.
How you fix the issue depends on why it happened in the first place. For example, if an app crashing is the cause, then a restart can do the trick. In case you're wondering, an app freezing or crashing can make your screen unresponsive because your touch input has to pass through the processor to reach the app.
A crash can jam the chains of that operation, halting the process. Just to be clear, not every unresponsive screen is a software issue; some need a professional repair.
Start with the basics
If your phone's screen suddenly becomes unresponsive to touch, start by examining it for cracks or other damage. If you see any, you're likely dealing with a hardware issue, not software. Next, take off the screen protector, since it can hide damage and could also be the cause of your screen's unresponsiveness. If you're wearing gloves, take them off.
Check what's around your screen too. Remove the case, disconnect any USB-C or Lightning accessories, and peel off any stickers covering the screen or sensors. Use a slightly damp microfiber cloth to properly clean your screen of dirt or liquid, and make sure to avoid getting moisture in your phone's opening.
If none of that works, the next step is to restart your phone. A good restart can clear any software glitch and set your phone's head straight. Since a standard restart is likely out of the question due to the screen not responding, you need to force restart your device. On an iPhone with Face ID, press and quickly release the volume up button. Then do the same with the volume down button. Next, press and hold the side button until the Apple logo appears. This could take longer than 10 seconds.
The process is different for older iPhone models. On an iPhone 7 and 7 Plus, press and hold the side and volume down button together. On an iPhone 6s and earlier, hold the Home button plus the side or top button.
On Android, the process can differ depending on the manufacturer, so you'll have to check for your specific device, but the standard process is to hold the power button for 30 seconds until it restarts.
Try safe mode and reset settings
If none of the earlier fixes get your screen working again, you're likely facing a deeper hardware or software issue. On Android, you can use safe mode to check whether a third-party app is behind your screen's unresponsiveness, because it loads only the software your device shipped with. If your screen responds in safe mode, then a third-party app is the culprit. If not, it's likely a hardware issue or, in some cases, a fault in the system software.
To enter safe mode, force restart the device. When the manufacturer's logo appears, press and hold the volume down button until the phone starts up. If successful, "Safe mode" will appear in the bottom-left corner.
Before concluding it's a hardware fault, try resetting your settings and turning off Developer options on your Android if it's on. To reset your iPhone's settings, open Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Reset > Reset All Settings. Note that Android steps vary by device.
For Samsung users, open Settings > General management > Reset > Reset all settings > Reset settings. If this doesn't work either, a factory reset is the last resort. On iPhone and Samsung, it's in the same menu as Reset settings.
Performing a factory reset wipes all data on your phone, so unless you have everything backed up or don't need the data on the device, we wouldn't advise doing this yet. Instead, take your device to your manufacturer's service center or a credible independent repairer and let them check if your screen has a hardware fault.
Some of these steps need a screen that responds at least a little, but if that's not the case, you may need to try mirroring your device.
How to mirror your phone if the screen is unresponsive to touch
Screen mirroring is a good way to get around an unresponsive screen, especially if it's damaged. Unfortunately, this method only works if you set it up earlier, when your screen was still responsive.
If you use the classic iPhone and Mac combo, then mirroring your iPhone is straightforward. Your iPhone needs to be locked and nearby, and your Mac needs macOS Sequoia or later, with either Apple silicon or an Apple T2 security chip. Both devices also need to have Bluetooth and Wi-Fi turned on. Then, click iPhone Mirroring in your Mac's Dock.
With that, you can use your iPhone even while the screen is unresponsive. For iPhone users who rock Windows, there's no official way to mirror and control your iPhone on Windows. Sadly, most third-party solutions are limited to viewing and can't control the iPhone.
For Android x Windows users, the Phone Link app is your best choice. Open the Phone Link app on your PC, then click "Open Phone screen." You may be asked to unlock your device, and both devices need to be on the same Wi-Fi network.
Android and Mac users aren't left out. Although there's no official method, there are third-party tools that work well. Scrcpy is a free, open-source tool that works across macOS, Windows and Linux. It mirrors your Android device over USB or Wi-Fi and lets you control the device with your computer's keyboard and mouse. Just make sure you enable USB debugging beforehand.
Scrcpy also has an OTG mode that lets you control your phone with your computer's keyboard and mouse, no USB debugging needed. No computer? A USB OTG adapter lets you plug in and operate your device with a wired mouse.

How to mirror your phone if the screen is unresponsive to touch
Screen mirroring is a good way to get around an unresponsive screen, especially if it's damaged. Unfortunately, this method only works if you set it up earlier, when your screen was still responsive.
If you use the classic iPhone and Mac combo, then mirroring your iPhone is straightforward. Your iPhone needs to be locked and nearby, and your Mac needs macOS Sequoia or later, with either Apple silicon or an Apple T2 security chip. Both devices also need to have Bluetooth and Wi-Fi turned on. Then, click iPhone Mirroring in your Mac's Dock.
With that, you can use your iPhone even while the screen is unresponsive. For iPhone users who rock Windows, there's no official way to mirror and control your iPhone on Windows. Sadly, most third-party solutions are limited to viewing and can't control the iPhone.
For Android x Windows users, the Phone Link app is your best choice. Open the Phone Link app on your PC, then click "Open Phone screen." You may be asked to unlock your device, and both devices need to be on the same Wi-Fi network.
Android and Mac users aren't left out. Although there's no official method, there are third-party tools that work well. Scrcpy is a free, open-source tool that works across macOS, Windows and Linux. It mirrors your Android device over USB or Wi-Fi and lets you control the device with your computer's keyboard and mouse. Just make sure you enable USB debugging beforehand.
Scrcpy also has an OTG mode that lets you control your phone with your computer's keyboard and mouse, no USB debugging needed. No computer? A USB OTG adapter lets you plug in and operate your device with a wired mouse.

title_en: How building a cheap home server could save you money in the long run
title_fa: How building a cheap home server could save you money in the long run
excerpt_en: Using an old PC to create your own server can save you quite a bit of money through a couple of avenues. Here's what it can do.
excerpt_fa: Using an old PC to create your own server can save you quite a bit of money through a couple of avenues. Here's what it can do.
content_en:
How building a cheap home server could save you money in the long run
That hunk of plastic collecting dust in the basement might be more useful than you realized.
Being around technology or computers for any extended period of time means that you've likely accumulated a decent amount of hardware over the years. With new upgrades and changes to one's setup often comes a question about what to do with old stuff you don't use anymore, or what you can do with any new hardware you get your hands on.
It's a common question regarding what to do with old PCs or laptops, but one that has a few surprising answers. One that always springs to mind is the creation of a home server, which, if you're a family looking to build your own custom streaming hub or have your own free mass storage unit, is a fabulous bit of financial investment that could be immensely beneficial to you in the uncertain years ahead of us in the technology field.
Building a home server is also tantalizingly easy, as well, making the entire process one that is both painless and affordable. And in a time when things feel a bit more complex than they should, having something as straightforward as the construction of a media server that could save you money honestly feels like a slam dunk.
It can trim down your streaming services bill
In addition to your regular bills, one thing that most of us spend a lot of money on during each calendar month is streaming services. There are a lot of them, and nearly every major company in the world has decided to put a plus symbol next to its name in order to enter the streaming service arms race.
It can add up to quite a bit of money over four weeks, and one way to combat that is to build your own home server. With one of these at your disposal, your server becomes something of a custom media machine, where you can stream your own shows and movies as you please. It can greatly cut down on the number of streaming services you have, making things a little lighter on your wallet.
It's sometimes shocking to see how many streaming services a family of any size is subscribed to, and using a home server to offset that can really help you keep your monthly bill down to a more manageable number. Thanks to media servers like Plex, Jellyfin and countless other alternatives, you can populate your device with anything you want.
Great cost-cutting measures on mass storage
Huge parts of our personal lives are often stored in our digital archives, as so many of us have precious photos and videos logged on our devices. If you're someone who has a fairly hefty selection of files, or even just incredibly important documents, a home server can pull its weight by doubling as a mass storage device.
If you subscribe to any sort of cloud storage or data backup service, it can all start to add up over the year. With your own home server, you can cut those elements out, and the server itself can also be upgradeable over time. If you're ever in need of more storage, the act of buying more hard drives and installing them is a snap.
By resurrecting an old PC that's seen its last days as a daily, primary driver into a home server, you can save a fairly large chunk of cash on storage and home entertainment needs. It can also act as a sort of building block toward actual custom PC builds, and once you have a strong understanding of those things, you may find that you have quite a bit of extra cash in your account every month.

title_en: Why your Spotify might be using so much storage
title_fa: Why your Spotify might be using so much storage
excerpt_en: Spotify can be a storage hog if you don't have your device's settings optimized. Here's what you can do if Spotify is taking up too much storage.
excerpt_fa: Spotify can be a storage hog if you don't have your device's settings optimized. Here's what you can do if Spotify is taking up too much storage.
content_en:
Why your Spotify might be using so much storage
If you're running low on storage, it's worth checking to see if Spotify might be the culprit.
We're all getting tired of subscription-based services, but when it comes to music streaming, it's a little harder to give up. You can still purchase individual tracks and albums, but it's often more economical to subscribe to Apple Music or Spotify if you listen to a wide variety of music. Furthermore, with how fast and reliable mobile data has become, you can stream virtually any song you want on the go. This saves you the hassle of managing a local library of music on your phone, not to mention the storage space you could otherwise use for other apps and media files.
If you've recently been hit by the low-storage warning on your phone, you can find out exactly what's taking up so much space. On iOS, navigate to Settings > General > iPhone Storage. If you're using Android, the exact menu labels may vary depending on your phone's manufacturer, and the easiest way to find this information may be to simply search your phone for "Storage." For Samsung, look under Settings > Device care > Storage. For other Android devices, you can usually locate it under Settings > Storage or Settings > About Phone > Storage. Your phone might automatically sort your apps by how much storage they're occupying. If you spot Spotify near the top, there's a good chance that downloaded music or cached data is what's eating away at your phone's storage.
Android lets you clear an app's cache in just a few taps. Navigate to something like Settings > Apps > See all apps > Spotify > Storage & cache and tap on Clear cache. Though you can nuke your entire offline music library by tapping on the Clear storage button, this will also sign you out of the app. Instead, the Spotify app offers a much better way to manage your downloads.
Manage your Spotify downloads
In the Spotify app on Android and iOS, you can check what music you have downloaded by navigating to the Your Library tab and tapping on Downloaded at the top. Here, you can pick individual playlists or albums and tap on the green download button to remove them from your device. This is a good way to free up storage by deleting the songs you don't want available offline, while keeping the stuff you do listen to more frequently.
You can, however, delete all downloads if you want to reclaim as much storage on your phone as possible. In the Spotify app, tap on your profile picture in the top-left corner of the screen. Navigate to Settings and privacy > Data-saving and offline, scroll all the way down and tap on Remove next to the Remove all downloads option. You can also clear Spotify's cache here.
You might need to restart your phone if you don't immediately see the freed-up storage reflected in your phone's settings. Other streaming services like Apple Music and Netflix also let you remove downloads — you just have to look for the option within the app's settings.
If you're using the Spotify app on a Windows or macOS computer, you can clear downloads by clicking on your profile picture, navigating to Settings, scrolling all the way down to the Storage section and clicking on Remove all downloads. Those who use Spotify on the web shouldn't have to worry about downloads taking up device storage, since the browser version doesn't support offline listening to begin with.
Adjust media quality on Spotify
If you do need an offline music library so you can listen to your tracks without an internet connection, you can still clear some storage space by adjusting the quality of your downloaded songs. On Android and iOS, launch Spotify and head to Settings and privacy > Media quality and scroll to the Download quality section. You can choose the Low option, then tap on the Download button next to the Update existing downloads option. Spotify says tracks downloaded or streamed in the Low quality setting are equivalent to around 24 kbps, which shouldn't be too bad for casual listening.
It's also worth noting that if you have the Lossless quality preset selected for your downloads, your offline music library is going to occupy significantly more storage. Lossless tracks are much larger than their compressed counterparts. While lossless audio can upgrade your music listening experience if you're using wired headphones and a DAC, the difference might not be noticeable if you usually opt for wireless earbuds.
I tested just how big of a difference downloading the same set of songs in different quality presets can make. With my music library downloaded in Lossless quality, Spotify was occupying around 22GB of space on my phone. When set to the Low preset, my entire music library fit in a little over 2GB — those are massive storage savings, and I didn't even have to give up offline listening. Periodically clearing Spotify's cache can also free up a noticeable amount of storage space.

title_en: How long is too long for a USB cable?
title_fa: How long is too long for a USB cable?
excerpt_en: USB cables, much like their HDMI cousins, have limits on how long they can be. The thing is, those limits are probably much lower than you expected.
excerpt_fa: USB cables, much like their HDMI cousins, have limits on how long they can be. The thing is, those limits are probably much lower than you expected.
content_en:
How long is too long for a USB cable?
One of the best things about USB is that you rarely need to think about it. Sure, there are some differences between USB generations, but no matter what, if you plug a USB cable into a compatible device, it will work without issues, as long as the cable isn't too long, that is. Of course, you're unlikely to need an extremely lengthy USB cable — unlike, say, HDMI cables — but if you ever do, there are limits to USB cable length that you should be aware of.
The USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF), which defines USB standards, has outlined maximum lengths for different types of USB cables. These range from about 16 feet to as low as 3 feet. The Forum is an industry group, not a regulatory body, so there's nothing stopping manufacturers from making longer cables. The limits are a guide to best practices, as exceeding the USB-IF's specifications could hamper a USB cable's performance.
USB transfer speeds suffer with longer cables
Each generation of USB cables can transfer data faster than the last, but later generations actually have a shorter recommended length. USB 1.0 and 2.0 cables have a recommended maximum of 16.4 feet. For USB 3.0 through 3.2, that drops to 9.8 feet. USB 4 cables are much more limited, with a maximum recommended length of just 2.6 feet. Whether you're using a USB-A or USB-C cable doesn't matter; the maximum length is the same either way.
It might seem odd that maximum cable length doesn't improve over time as transfer rate does, but it has to do with the physical limits of the cables. A signal traveling through a cable degrades over time due to electrical resistance. The farther a signal has to travel, the more cable it has to push through to get there, losing signal along the way. Longer cables are also more susceptible to damage, which can further slow transfer speeds.
A USB cable that's too long won't suddenly stop working. Instead, it simply won't function as well as one that's within spec. Data may transfer more slowly than you're used to, or connected devices won't receive as much power. The higher the potential transfer rate or power delivery, the more you're likely to notice the difference. That's why it's important to know the maximum length of your USB cables.
How to extend the range of a USB cable
If you can, it's always best to reposition your devices so you don't need to exceed a USB cable's length limits, but that's not always possible. In those cases, you can purchase an active USB cable or an active USB extender, either of which will have built-in components to extend the signal's range. However, active USB cables are significantly more expensive than standard cables. They also draw extra power from the USB port, and thus might not be compatible with older ports.
Another potential solution is to use a powered USB hub and use the longest supported cable between the hub and your computer. Plugging too many devices into the same hub can slow them down, but as long as you don't exceed the USB port's bandwidth, you shouldn't encounter any noticeable performance difference. Powered hubs are preferable, since an unpowered hub can only draw power from the USB port, which can be unreliable.

title_en: OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round
title_fa: OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round
excerpt_en: OpenAI’s latest funding round doesn't seem to be living up to expectations.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI’s latest funding round doesn't seem to be living up to expectations.
content_en:
OpenAI’s latest funding round isn’t quite living up to expectations, according to multiple news reports.
OpenAI was previously reported to be raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, and then at a $1.25 trillion valuation, ahead of a planned IPO. But The Financial Times reported Friday that the company has subsequently lowered its funding target to $20 billion, with a first close that’s expected to be even lower than that.
The round will be led by a group of investors from the United Arab Emirates, the FT said. A subsequent retail offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total funding amount to the $20 billion target.
A follow-up story in The Wall Street Journal offered more details, namely that the company has secured $11 billion so far, and that its fundraising efforts had met with a “tepid” response from some large investors.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment. The company’s reported funding challenges could be blamed, in part, on bad timing, as Wall Street investors have become wary of heavy AI infrastructure spending, leading to a major sell off of tech stocks. And Anthropic’s planned IPO could be facing challenges, too.

content_en:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

content_fa:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
We have Muse Charm at home.
But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

title_en: From restaurant guides to payments, here’s how TikTok is building a super app
title_fa: From restaurant guides to payments, here’s how TikTok is building a super app
excerpt_en: TikTok may be working to become the app that people use for most of their digital activities.
excerpt_fa: TikTok may be working to become the app that people use for most of their digital activities.
content_en:
TikTok announced this week that it’s adding an in-app restaurant guide, marking another step in the platform’s expansion beyond social media. The company has also recently been spotted developing a feature that would allow users to send money over direct messages.
The social media app has steadily expanded its offerings in recent years, adding TikTok Shop, a map for local discovery, more robust search features, games, and more. It appears that TikTok is taking steps to evolve into a “super app,” a single platform where users can do much more than just watch and share videos and that can actually handle a wide range of needs in one destination.
The super app model is big in China with apps like WeChat, which is kind of like Facebook, WhatsApp, Apple Pay, and an app store all rolled into a single platform. Of course, there’s the question of whether a super app model would work outside of China, but that doesn’t mean TikTok won’t try.
Instead of switching between apps, TikTok is working to become the app that people use for most of their digital activities. After taking its biggest leap with TikTok Shop, the company — which, notably, transitioned to new, primarily U.S. ownership back in January — has applied the same playbook to recent developments.
Restaurant Guides
TikTok has become a popular destination for restaurant recommendations, with viral videos often driving customers to local eateries. Now, the platform is looking to make that discovery process even easier with a new feature called “Must Eat.” The community-driven guide highlights restaurants getting attention on the platform.
“Must Eat” draws on more than 40 million posts and comments to compile restaurant recommendations and curated lists in one place. Users can browse restaurants by city and narrow their search by cuisine, price, rating, and location.
The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google Maps. It also reflects how the app is expanding its role in users’ everyday decisions, from what they buy to where they choose to go out to eat.
Payments
Bloomberg reported in August that TikTok is developing a feature that would allow users to send each other money via direct messages. If rolled out, the feature would use the social media service’s TikTok Pay offering, which is already available in Southeast Asia for TikTok Shop purchases.
Additionally, Reuters reported in March that TikTok had applied to Brazil’s central bank for approval to operate as a financial technology company offering lending and payment services.
TikTok’s potential expansion into payments marks a significant way that the company is branching out beyond a social media platform and into a digital ecosystem. By aiming to bring financial services into its app, TikTok is looking to increase user engagement, open new revenue streams, and position itself to compete with fintech startups and e-commerce platforms.
Sports
Over the years, TikTok has steadily been looking to become a place where users can come for sports highlights and content. In early June, the company launched a dedicated hub for the FIFA World Cup where users can see scores, match schedules, standings, trending videos, highlights, videos from players, and more.
If people are already watching videos on TikTok but want to keep up with the score, they can do so without leaving the app or opening a dedicated sports news app or Google.
The World Cup hub was made possible through TikTok’s Sports-focused product called “TikTok GamePlan,” which is designed to allow sports teams, leagues, and broadcasters to drive discovery and engagement on the platform. The social media giant also has partnerships with Major League Soccer (MLS) and Major League Baseball (MLB) for behind-the-scenes and exclusive content.
Hotel and attraction booking
In May, TikTok launched TikTok GO, a way for users to discover and book hotels, attractions, and experiences directly within its app in the United States. TikTok GO surfaces lodging and things to do through videos, search, and location pages. When users find something they’re interested in, they can view details, check availability, and complete a booking.
Instead of directing users to third-party websites after they find a destination or recommendation in a video, TikTok has started positioning itself as a one-stop platform where viral travel content can drive bookings and revenue.
While people have already been using TikTok as a search engine and replacement for Google, this latest step puts TikTok in more direct competition with Google’s core businesses, Search and Google Maps, because it’s working to not only be the app where you discover places, but also the platform where you purchase that trip.
TikTok Shop
It’s widely known that one of TikTok’s biggest leaps beyond social media was the launch of TikTok Shop. TikTok began testing TikTok Shop in 2021 and launched it in the U.S. in 2023. Since then, the company has been able to successfully compete with Amazon, Shein, and other online marketplaces.
According to eMarketer, TikTok Shop grew its U.S. sales by 407% in 2024 and another 108% in 2025 to reach $15.82 billion. As of last year, the company accounted for 18.2% of total social commerce in the U.S., with that number expected to reach 24.1% by 2027.
Additionally, TikTok began challenging digital marketplaces even further with the launch of TikTok Shop gift cards late last year. TikTok Shop has also recently expanded into luxury retail, after initially mainly being known for cheap goods.
Music
TikTok’s popularity has influenced the music industry and how people discover new music, and the company tried to capitalize on this by launching a streaming service called TikTok Music in 2023 to take on platforms like Spotify and Apple Music, but ended up shutting it down a year later.

excerpt_en: The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode. The search improvements are quite...
excerpt_fa: The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode. The search improvements are quite...
content_en:
The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode.
Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
The latest Windows Insider builds revamp search with filters, actions, and phone controls.
The latest Windows Insider builds revamp search with filters, actions, and phone controls.
The search improvements are quite comprehensive. You can now filter results for files, actions, or web results. You can also use the search box to perform actions like changing the screen brightness or volume, and even perform actions on a connected phone, including making calls. Results can also offer much more detail, like when a file was last modified and its author, or pull in charts for stock prices and weather forecasts. And you can train Windows 11 search by clicking inline thumbs-up or thumbs-down icons to help it improve over time.
For the full list of changes, check out Microsoft’s blog post. Beta Build 26220.9836 and Experimental Build 26340.9843 are both available now to Windows Insiders.

content_en:
While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page.
Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
You have options for preordering the new MacBook Pro, but only one retailer is offering this sweet perk.
You have options for preordering the new MacBook Pro, but only one retailer is offering this sweet perk.
My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions.

excerpt_en: Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it's hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape, which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced...
excerpt_fa: Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it's hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape, which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced...
content_en:
Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it’s hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape, which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced single “Down On My Luck”? Maybe you didn’t even realize that Mensa was a rapper. Maybe you know him from his roles on The Chi or Bel-Air. Or perhaps you’re mostly aware of him through his activism, social media presence (peeling oranges and waxing poetic), or his podcast The Vic Mensa Show.
Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
Between his music, acting, podcast, activism, and businesses, Vic Mensa wears a lot of hats.
Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
Between his music, acting, podcast, activism, and businesses, Vic Mensa wears a lot of hats.
Point is, the man wears many hats. Part of the secret to being so prolific, it turns out, is Voice Memos. Just capture those ideas before they disappear.
What is your most indispensable tool?
Voice Memos. Everything starts there for me. Songs, essay ideas, orange tree thoughts, voice notes to myself at some wild hour, little things my son says that I do not want to lose. My phone is a million distractions in one rectangle, but Voice Memos is one of the few parts of it that still feels honest. Just press record before the thought disappears.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
Instagram, for better or worse. That’s definitely where my voice has really found its legs. I started out peeling an orange and talking through whatever was on my mind, and it turned into this whole conversation with people about politics, history, music, grief, jokes, fatherhood, all of it. That response helped show me there was room for The Vic Mensa Show too. Instagram can be a circus, obviously, but it’s also a very valuable tool for connection.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Maybe Meta glasses. Them motherfuckers seem like they’re being used for evil.
What creation are you most proud of?
Probably my upcoming album right now. It’s the first album that I’ve really taken myself completely seriously as a producer. The surrounding art, videos, design, clothing, and world I’m building around it is something that really excites me as well.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I either do my Shambhavi Mahamudra meditation that I learned from Sadhguru or the Wim Hof breathing method. Ideally, I’ll do the Wim Hof breathing method in the steam room and then the meditation.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Anything that touches your life every day. A good mattress. Good headphones. Quality food. Clothes you will actually keep for years. Experiences with your child. I have wasted money on plenty of dumb shit, so I am trying to be better about buying things that either last or make a real memory.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Live from the contradiction.
What is the last GIF or meme you used?

Anything that touches your life every day. A good mattress. Good headphones. Quality food. Clothes you will actually keep for years. Experiences with your child. I have wasted money on plenty of dumb shit, so I am trying to be better about buying things that either last or make a real memory.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Live from the contradiction.
