In other words, Rivian is losing less than it did a year ago because they sold more cars and made more money per vehicle. (Also, the company continued to sell pollution credits to other carmakers, and also received a tariff refund from the government — all of which was recorded as revenue.)
Rivian is losing less than it did a year ago because they sold more cars and made more money per vehicle.
Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin. Most of this cash came from licensing their tech to Volkswagen, alongside customer subscriptions for Rivian’s Autonomy Plus driving features. In many ways, Rivian’s tech partnership with Volkswagen and software sales are currently paying the bills, keeping the company profitable overall while it absorbs a lot of heavy upfront costs from launching the R2.
Earlier this month, Rivian reported a record sales quarter, with 19,751 vehicles produced and 19,248 delivered. That represents an 85 percent year-over-year increase in production and a 45 percent jump in deliveries. (For a direct-to-consumer automaker like Rivian, deliveries serve as a proxy for sales.)
Rivian doesn’t break down sales by model, so we don’t exactly how many R2s have reached customers so far. But the company said that the R2 is now the “best-selling Rivian vehicle by volume,” outselling the R1T and R1S, as well as the Electric Delivery Van (EDV).
“We had great results with R2 becoming our best selling vehicle by volume in the third quarter,” Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said in a statement, ahead of the company’s earnings call this afternoon. “Customer and media feedback on R2 has been exceptional.”
The R2 was designed from the ground up to be Rivian’s higher-volume, mass-market offering — and by overtaking the company’s more expensive, lower-volume legacy vehicles, it seems to be doing just that. Still, the R2 isn’t bringing in the bulk of the revenue yet, as indicated by Rivian’s use of the phrase “by volume.” Most of the money is still coming from the VW partnership and its software division.
But that could change once Rivian starts shipping the more affordable versions of the R2, like the $55,485 Premium trim (coming in late 2026), the $49,985 Standard Long-Range (early 2027), and the $46,495 Standard (late 2027).

title_en: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
title_fa: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
excerpt_en: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
content_en:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.
Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.
As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.
Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.
AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards.
Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company.

title_en: Popcorn bucket innovation is at an all-time low and the Dune: Part Three 'Double Sandworm' is proof
title_fa: Popcorn bucket innovation is at an all-time low and the Dune: Part Three 'Double Sandworm' is proof
excerpt_en: Just what the Sandworm bucket needed: a second hole.
excerpt_fa: Just what the Sandworm bucket needed: a second hole.
content_en:
Popcorn bucket innovation is at an all-time low and the Dune: Part Three 'Double Sandworm' is proof
Where is the imagination?
Collectible popcorn buckets have become a fixture of movie theaters' post-pandemic recovery, and if hawking plastic helps them keep the lights on, so be it. But if we are going to submit ourselves to the Funko Pop-ification of food receptacles, shouldn't they at least be interesting?
Two years after Dune: Part Two's Sandworm popcorn bucket went viral, AMC Theatres made the obvious decision to double down for Dune: Part Three. The theater chain is selling two themed buckets for the film's release, the "Sandworm Thumper" and "Double Sandworm," each with a worm-shaped hand hole (the Double, naturally, has two).
An epic conclusion calls for legendary collectibles. See DUNE: PART THREE and seize control of your collection, including AMC Theatres exclusives on 12/17. Take a sneak peek now. 👀 https://t.co/XIUIke0xaZ pic.twitter.com/h0xjF4WwWS
— AMC Theatres (@AMCTheatres) October 29, 2026
Adding a second hole solves one of the original bucket's problems by letting two people reach for popcorn at the same time, while underlining the sexual innuendo many people found implicit in the original bucket's orifice. It's also completely uninspired.
You can get a lot of mileage out of serving popcorn out of an unusually shaped box. AMC was right to think it would be funny to eat out of a handbag while watching The Devil Wears Prada 2. It's hard not to love the Trojan Horse bucket sold for The Odyssey. Even the "Guile Hair" wearable popcorn bucket the company sold alongside Street Fighter has some charm. But those are the exceptions, and novelty can only take you so far.
Is it actually fun to reach on top of your head for popcorn more than once? Is adding a second hole the best AMC could come up with to capture the spirit of one of the more visually striking blockbuster franchises in recent memory? Should anyone in their right mind pay $35 for a bowl with a lumpy hand in it that says "Clayface" on the side? I don't think so.
One reason the original Sandworm bucket might have connected is that its creators somehow didn't anticipate people would immediately see it as a sex toy. It was weird, seemingly by accident. Most popcorn buckets released since don't appear to be made with that same level of childlike naivete, and they're worse for it.

title_en: GM to pay $220 million to resolve claims it sold driving habits data
title_fa: GM to pay $220 million to resolve claims it sold driving habits data
excerpt_en: General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers, as reported earlier by Reuters. The agreement, which resolves a complaint from a coalition of 36 US attorneys general, requires GM to limit the...
excerpt_fa: General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers, as reported earlier by Reuters. The agreement, which resolves a complaint from a coalition of 36 US attorneys general, requires GM to limit the...
content_en:
General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers, as reported earlier by Reuters. The agreement, which resolves a complaint from a coalition of 36 US attorneys general, requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.
GM to pay $220 million to resolve claims it sold driving habits data
A coalition of 36 state attorneys general secured the settlement, which also requires GM to limit the data it collects.
A coalition of 36 state attorneys general secured the settlement, which also requires GM to limit the data it collects.
The allegations surround GM’s now-discontinued Smart Driver program, which collected data about driving habits, including acceleration, braking, and trip length. GM allegedly passed this information to data brokers, enabling insurance companies to purchase the data and raise premiums. The states also accused GM of failing to notify drivers that they were enrolled in its Smart Driver program, and that the carmaker was collecting their data.
“This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices,” GM spokesperson Charlotte McCoy said in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”
This settlement comes just months after GM agreed to pay $12.75 million to settle similar claims in California. Oregon AG Dan Rayfield and Washington AG Nick Brown co-led the states’ case against GM, which also included New York, Florida, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and many others.
“People bought a car, not a tracking device,” Rayfield says in a press release. “GM told drivers this program would help them drive more safely and promised it wouldn’t share their data with insurers without permission. Our investigation found GM sold that data anyway, and some drivers paid for it with higher premiums.”
Update, October 29th: Added a statement from GM.

title_en: Where was my invite to the — wait, what? Airbnb had a gala?
title_fa: Where was my invite to the — wait, what? Airbnb had a gala?
excerpt_en: Airbnb’s nonprofit held its inaugural gala on Wednesday in Los Angeles, and the internet had one reaction — the *what* gala?
excerpt_fa: Airbnb’s nonprofit held its inaugural gala on Wednesday in Los Angeles, and the internet had one reaction — the *what* gala?
content_en:
Airbnb’s nonprofit held its inaugural gala on Wednesday in Los Angeles, and the internet had one reaction — the what gala?
In case you missed it, back in 2020, Airbnb launched a nonprofit that provides free and temporary housing to families impacted by crisis or disaster. Its gala makes sense, actually, in that significant causes often throw splashy events to please big donors.
In a press release shared with TechCrunch this week, Airbnb noted that the gala marked the launch of a new initiative for the nonprofit, in which Airbnb will start donating a portion of its commercial revenue from each stay booked starting from the day of the gala, October 28. The cut amounts to 10 cents, to be exact, but Airbnb did make $12.2 billion in revenue last year.
This initiative will help generate $500 million that will then go to the nonprofit over the next five years to help it provide free housing for 1 million nights each year, per the release. It will also let the company expand to supporting families also facing displacement due to domestic violence, veterans in need, or those traveling for medical needs.
A spokesperson for Airbnb said that the night was for its supporters and “marking the next chapter of our work.” Airbnb said that people had the option to donate, but “fundraising wasn’t the focus of the evening” and that the nonprofit “didn’t set a fundraising target.” The idea is for the Gala to happen each year, and last night was invite-only, the spokesperson said, with no tables or seats sold.
The gala was hosted by Jimmy Kimmel, with a live performance by Charli XCX, and food was curated by Chef José Andrés of World Central Kitchen. The guest list featured Serena Williams, Demi Lovato, Charlize Theron, and Cynthia Erivo. For the celebrities, it was a glamorous night in society for a helpful cause, joining the ranks of other Los Angeles events, like the Baby2Baby Gala and the Academy Museum Gala, as a place to be seen.
Still, people were literally confused as to why Airbnb was having a gala and how it attracted top-tier celebrities.
Again, a lovely event, and another data point showing that throwing a gala is one of the best ways to get rich people in a room to pay money and get media attention. And now a bunch of people on the internet know that Airbnb helps people in need, rather than perpetually making the news for negatively impacting the housing market.
This piece was updated.

title_en: Meta quietly launches an AI fashion app called Style Sketch
title_fa: Meta quietly launches an AI fashion app called Style Sketch
excerpt_en: The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve already shared, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.
excerpt_fa: The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve already shared, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.
content_en:
Meta has quietly launched Style Sketch, an AI fashion app that helps users put together outfit ideas using clothes they already own. The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve posted, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.
Style Sketch then suggests outfit combinations built from your wardrobe matched to your style. Users can then try on the outfits on a “realistic model matched to your body shape and skin tone,” the app description reads.
The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is available in Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand on iOS and Android.
Meta did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. It’s unknown whether Meta plans to launch Style Sketch more widely.
Several apps already use AI to help users digitize their wardrobes and visualize new outfits, including startups like Alta. Even Google Photos offers tools that let users turn photos of their clothes into digital closets where they can create new outfit ideas.
To compete with what’s already on the market, Meta will likely rely less on the novelty of the idea and more on the app’s integration with Instagram, where users already have a visual record of their personal style.
Rather than relying on random suggestions, users can also select a specific item from their wardrobe and get fresh outfit ideas built around it, according to the app description.
The app can also help users plan outfits for trips. If they enter their destination, trip length, and planned activities, users can get a day-by-day outfit plan that takes the weather forecast and itinerary into account.
Style Sketch is one of many AI apps from Meta in recent months. Most recently, the company launched an app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. Meta has also launched Pocket, a tool for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, which lets users quickly generate AI-powered videos.
The wave of new apps is part of a broader effort at Meta to release more apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that CEO Mark Zuckerberg told employees the company plans to release far more apps than it has historically, as AI-driven efficiencies have made it faster and easier to ship new apps.

title_en: Hacker may have stolen millions in a malware attack against online poker players
title_fa: Hacker may have stolen millions in a malware attack against online poker players
excerpt_en: Wired has the story of a superuser cheating scandal.
excerpt_fa: Wired has the story of a superuser cheating scandal.
content_en:
Hacker may have stolen millions in a malware attack against online poker players
Wired has the story of a superuser cheating scandal.
Professional poker is the latest community to reckon with the impact of a high-profile cyberattack. Wired reports that hundreds of online poker players have allegedly been targeted in a malware attack that allowed a cheater to see their screens.
Cases where a player manages to cheat by getting unfair access to another person's cards is known as the "superuser" strategy, and it has popped up from time to time in the poker scene over the years. This most recent attack appears to have been a long-term campaign that may have seen millions of dollars stolen from across major online poker platforms. The Wired story claims that the hacker exploited third-party tools allowing people to run multiple poker games at once to install a malware program called MeshAgent on specific players' computers.
Different online poker platforms reportedly displayed a range of responses, which is especially surprising since the hacker's real name is known by the community. Wired did not publish the cheater's identity since they have not been charged with a crime, and the individual did not respond to the publication's requests for comment.
One service had banned the cheater before the MeshAgent hack was publicly uncovered based on the account having an anomalously high win rate and play tendencies. Others released tools to help players check if their machines had been compromised after the malware was found. But one company not only allowed the cheater to remain active despite complaints made by other players, but further claimed that it found no evidence of compromised game outcomes and would not refund players for their losses.
The entire Wired profile is a fascinating read for cybersecurity and poker fans alike. It's also just the latest reminder to take basic protective actions to keep you and your hardware safe.

excerpt_fa: Now you can generate, preview, and edit PDFs, Google Docs, Google Sheets, slide decks, Markdown files, TXT files, and code directly within Google Gemini. The new file editing capabilities are available starting today for all Gemini users, and while PDF previews/editing works on...
content_en:
Now you can generate, preview, and edit PDFs, Google Docs, Google Sheets, slide decks, Markdown files, TXT files, and code directly within Google Gemini. The new file editing capabilities are available starting today for all Gemini users, and while PDF previews/editing works on both the web and mobile, all other file formats are only in the web version for now.
You can generate and edit Google Docs files directly in Gemini chats now
Editing files you generate with Gemini no longer requires leaving the app.
Editing files you generate with Gemini no longer requires leaving the app.
Google added support for generating and downloading files in Gemini earlier this year, but now you can tweak those files without leaving the Gemini app. Google says you can expand documents to edit them in full-screen mode and highlight text in files to ask Gemini questions or prompt it to make changes to the file, like highlighting a table and asking Gemini to turn it into a graph.
You could already use Gemini to edit files with its integrations in Google’s Workspace apps, like the Gemini bar in Google Docs. Anthropic also launched a feature earlier this year that allows users to generate and edit documents and presentations in Claude chats.

content_en:
Netflix is making a live-action PUBG show written and directed by Donald Glover
The streamer also has an Assassin's Creed series in the works, along with a Gears of War feature film.
Netflix is making a live-action series based on the massively popular battle royale game PUBG. The whole thing is being spearheaded by Donald Glover. That's right. The guy who made Atlanta is making a PUBG show.
According to Netflix, Glover will star in, write, direct and executive produce the project. He will be assisted by frequent collaborator and sibling Stephen Glover.
On the surface, this seems like an odd move for Glover. Atlanta was a highly-regarded and occasionally experimental meditation on the American dream. PUBG is a game in which 100 people try to shoot one another for loot and the promise of a chicken dinner.
There isn't much of a story, however, which gives Glover plenty of room to get creative with the source material. The game does hint that this is a bloodsport tournament of some kind to entertain elites, which could mean the show will have a Squid Game or even Hunger Games type vibe. We'll have to wait and see.
We don't have any casting details, beyond Glover himself. There's no release window just yet. It's also entirely possible the team will make a pilot and the suits at Netflix will kill it. This recently happened with the Buffy the Vampire Slayer reboot at Hulu, despite Chloé Zhao's involvement. Atlanta won seven Emmys and was nominated for 26, so I say let the man do what he wants.
This is just the latest video game adaptation that Netflix has greenlit. It's making a live-action series based on Assassin's Creed and a feature length movie based on Gears of War.

title_en: Don't expect more Assassin's Creed remakes anytime soon
title_fa: Don't expect more Assassin's Creed remakes anytime soon
excerpt_en: Ubisoft shared some updates on the franchise, including confirmation of a New Game+ option for Assassin's Creed Valhalla.
excerpt_fa: Ubisoft shared some updates on the franchise, including confirmation of a New Game+ option for Assassin's Creed Valhalla.
content_en:
Don't expect more Assassin's Creed remakes anytime soon
Ubisoft shared some updates on the franchise, including confirmation of a New Game+ option for Assassin's Creed Valhalla.
Ubisoft offered Assassin's Creed fans a string of franchise updates on Thursday, including one that might come as a disappointment for many. The company said that, despite the success of the enjoyable Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, it doesn't have any other remakes in the works right now.
"One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development," the company wrote in a blog post. "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories."
Ubisoft said it learned a lot from its work on Black Flag Resynced. "Rebuilding old systems from scratch, adding new elements that fit the experience and balancing legacy with innovation was a massive undertaking," it wrote. The company noted that while it's focusing on new Assassin's Creed titles for now, it's open to eventually revisiting older games.
Earlier this week, Ubisoft released the final major update for Black Flag Resynced, which included New Game+ and a higher difficulty level. It also announced a New Game+ option for 2020's Assassin's Creed Valhalla, which will be available on November 5. Ubisoft will share more in the coming days, including details on updates for current-gen consoles.
As for upcoming games, Ubisoft stated that the multiplayer Assassin's Creed project, dubbed Codename Invictus, "is now evolving in an exciting direction" that includes more of the series' hallmarks following feedback from a playtest. It's also making steady progress on Codename Hexe, the next mainline entry in the series. It plans to share its next major update about this "darker Assassin's Creed experience" in 2027.
Elsewhere, Ubisoft said production has almost wrapped on Netflix's live-action Assassin's Creed series. A release window hasn't been announced yet. In addition, the franchise will celebrate its 20th anniversary in 2027. Ubisoft said you can expect "a year of reveals, updates, rewards and community moments."

title_en: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese government spy
title_fa: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese government spy
excerpt_en: President Trump reportedly chose to do nothing in response.
excerpt_fa: President Trump reportedly chose to do nothing in response.
content_en:
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese government spy
President Trump reportedly chose to do nothing in response.
As if Big Tech in 2026 wasn't already crazy enough, we can now add "Jensen Huang espionage scandal" to the list. The New York Times reports that US officials see the NVIDIA CEO as the target of a Chinese government spy. Wilder still, the report says that President Trump was briefed on the matter a year ago and decided to just... do nothing.
US intelligence agencies reportedly surveilled Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen Huang), a Chinese citizen and executive at Singapore data center firm Megaspeed. That surveillance turned up contact with an American citizen, later identified as Jensen Huang.
America's spy agencies concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing. Before the espionage allegations turned up, she was already suspected of helping steer advanced NVIDIA chips into China. Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion in NVIDIA-based equipment in under two years. The Times describes that as an unusual amount of business for a small and obscure company.
A thin public profile and a baffling White House response
Alice Huang's public profile is thin. She described herself as Megaspeed's CEO. The company reportedly listed her as its managing director for its first eight months before removing her from that role in its corporate paperwork. A Chinese investment fund where she worked described her as a former TV reporter, but The Times was unable to verify that background.
The above photo was posted to NetThunder's LinkedIn account in 2024, just before Megaspeed began those big chip purchases. It shows Alice Huang sitting close to Jensen Huang, who is drinking with other AI executives.
The CEO of the world's most valuable chip company being targeted by a Chinese government spy op is a wild story, but not a shocking one. The truly crazy part is that President Trump reportedly took no action. Jensen Huang reportedly never even got a "defensive briefing," a standard heads-up sometimes given to Americans being targeted by foreign spies.
It isn't clear why. The Times notes Trump has been wary of anything that might disrupt NVIDIA's chip sales or further complicate trade with China. (Never mind that he launched the trade war with China with his tariffs.) The report added that it's unclear whether officials worried that briefing Jensen Huang might tip off Alice Huang, who is still said to be under surveillance. The report doesn't say what information she may have passed to Beijing.
There's much more to sift through in the Times' full report.

title_en: Meta will now alert parents if teens 'repeatedly' search for self-harm content on Facebook
title_fa: Meta will now alert parents if teens 'repeatedly' search for self-harm content on Facebook
excerpt_en: The company will also notify parents about conversations with Meta AI.
excerpt_fa: The company will also notify parents about conversations with Meta AI.
content_en:
Meta will now alert parents if teens 'repeatedly' search for self-harm content on Facebook
The company will also notify parents about conversations with Meta AI.
Meta is now expanding its parental notifications that appear when teens search for content related to suicide and self-harm. After adding the alerts to Instagram earlier this year, the company is now rolling out similar capabilities to parents who supervise teens with Facebook accounts, as well as chats with its AI assistant.
With the update, Meta will notify parents if their teen "repeatedly" searches for self-harm content "within a short period of time." Likewise, if a teen chats with Meta AI in a way that "suggests they may be at risk of suicide or self-harm," parents will also be notified.
The company is intentionally vague about what the exact criteria are for triggering these notifications. It previously said it "chose a threshold that requires a few searches within a short period of time, while still erring on the side of caution" and that it hoped to "avoid sending these notifications unnecessarily." Should a teen meet that threshold, parents receive an alert via text, email or WhatsApp, and a push notification in their own app. The alerts don't detail the specific search terms or contents of Meta AI chats, but recommend that parents speak with their teens. It also provides resources for helplines.
The feature is part of Meta's push to enroll teens into parent-supervised "teen accounts" that give caregivers more control over teens' privacy settings. The accounts are also meant to limit teens' ability to see sensitive content, including self-harm-related posts, and interact with adults.
If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org

excerpt_en: With its playful design, versatility, and relatively affordable price, the Ikea Varmblixt quickly became one of my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy’s new favorite smart light products when she tested it in April. Now, the donut-shaped lamp is on sale for $79.99 ($20 off)...
excerpt_fa: With its playful design, versatility, and relatively affordable price, the Ikea Varmblixt quickly became one of my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy’s new favorite smart light products when she tested it in April. Now, the donut-shaped lamp is on sale for $79.99 ($20 off)...
content_en:
With its playful design, versatility, and relatively affordable price, the Ikea Varmblixt quickly became one of my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy’s new favorite smart light products when she tested it in April. Now, the donut-shaped lamp is on sale for $79.99 ($20 off) through November 11th at Ikea.
Ikea’s colorful donut-shaped smart lamp is $20 off
The Varmblixt can display hundreds of colors thanks to its Matter support, and can be put on your table or wall
The Varmblixt can display hundreds of colors thanks to its Matter support, and can be put on your table or wall
Don’t let us tell you where you can or cannot put your Varmblixt. But it’s meant to sit on a table or be mounted on a wall (it can hang from a drilled-in screw, nothing fancy). At just 180 lumens, it isn’t particularly bright, so it’s better suited for use as a bedside lamp or for mood lighting than being tasked to illuminate a room. The newer model lets you cycle through 12 preset colors, including shades of pink, blue, green, and white, as opposed to just orange with the predecessor. The included wireless remote lets you switch between colors, adjust the brightness, and turn the lamp on or off without needing an app or a separate hub (there’s a power button on the lamp itself) . You can also use the remote to control other compatible Ikea lights.
For those who want to embed the Varmblixt into their smart home setup, the lamp supports Matter, allowing it to work with compatible smart home platforms including Apple Home, Google Home, and Amazon Alexa. In addition to letting you control the lights with your voice, this gives you access to hundreds more colors, lets you set lighting schedules and sleep or wake-up routines, and allows you to connect the lamp with motion sensors and other smart lights you may have. You can unlock those features with Ikea’s Dirigera hub, as well, which also offers a feature through its Home Smart app that gradually adjusts the shade of white throughout the day akin to natural daylight.

title_en: Granola crunches up a dictation feature to compete with Wispr
title_fa: Granola crunches up a dictation feature to compete with Wispr
excerpt_en: Uno reverse! After Wispr added meeting notes to its dictation app, Granola is adding dictation to its meeting notetaker. The voice AI wars are getting interesting.
excerpt_fa: Uno reverse! After Wispr added meeting notes to its dictation app, Granola is adding dictation to its meeting notetaker. The voice AI wars are getting interesting.
content_en:
Apps in the consumer voice AI world seem to be converging, as Granola, known for its meeting notetaker, launched a dictation feature today. This comes months after Wispr, known for its dictation tool, launched a meeting notetaker.
Granola’s dictation currently works on Mac just like any other such tool. Users can press the “Fn” key and start speaking, and the tool cleans up and formats their speech and posts the final text. This feature works across all apps, so users can post notes, dictate prompts, and reply to emails and messages. The startup said that dictation is available for all plans without any limits.
The company said that the feature will land on iOS and Windows soon.
Granola and Wispr are valued at $1.5 billion and $2 billion, respectively. Granola is focused on meeting-related automation and notetaking. On the other hand, Wispr is trying to build its own models through a research lab, which is exploring different human-computer interfaces.
The feature mashups are not exclusive to Granola and Wispr. Other voice startups such as Fireflies, Speechify, and Monologue have converged into multifeature apps with meeting notetaking and dictation capabilities. Until earlier in the year, the play was around having a focused app that does one thing well. But now, all of these apps are thinking about how to get more out of capturing users’ speech.

title_en: Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
title_fa: Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
excerpt_en: The new MacBook Pro brings with it a bunch of firsts for Apple laptops, the two flashiest being an OLED display and touchscreen functionality. But as an image-accuracy enthusiast, trained calibrator, and resident display expert, what excites me most about the MacBook Pro with...
excerpt_fa: The new MacBook Pro brings with it a bunch of firsts for Apple laptops, the two flashiest being an OLED display and touchscreen functionality. But as an image-accuracy enthusiast, trained calibrator, and resident display expert, what excites me most about the MacBook Pro with...
content_en:
The new MacBook Pro brings with it a bunch of firsts for Apple laptops, the two flashiest being an OLED display and touchscreen functionality. But as an image-accuracy enthusiast, trained calibrator, and resident display expert, what excites me most about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the technology it uses to display an accurate picture. It’s the first laptop, and only the second product overall, to support Apple CMF 2026 color modes. It could be the future for displays.
Apple’s new laptop supports one of the coolest features for color pros
CMFs, or color-matching functions, mathematically represent how we perceive color, and there are a few different variations. The specification that’s been the standard for years is CIE 1931 (CIE stands for Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage, or International Commission on Illumination). For nearly a century, CIE 1931 has been a reliable calibration target, and most of the reference modes on the new MacBook use it.
But with the development of new display technologies over the past 20 years that have ultra-narrow band spectra — such as OLED, LEDs with KSF phosphors, and quantum dots — CIE 1931’s shortcomings are increasingly apparent. Even when calibrated to the same D65 white point, the same image on an OLED and quantum dot LED can look identical to one person, but different to another because of biological variations in our eyes. We all have small discrepancies in our eyes — such as the sensitivity of the cones in our eyes, which allow us to see color — and those can change as we age. CIE 1931 doesn’t properly handle that and was created based on only 17 test subjects. It’s not ideal in a professional setting where content needs to look the same regardless of the screen technology it’s on or who’s viewing it. Apple CMF 2026 addresses that, so that displays look the same regardless of the technology they use.
Apple first included its new CMF on the Studio Display XDR, which I reviewed earlier this year and found to be an excellent, albeit expensive, monitor for color professionals because of Apple CMF 2026 and the reference color modes. But the fact that this technology is now on a laptop that’s portable and not just a standalone monitor living on a desk is a big help for professionals on the move.
As on the Studio Display XDR, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has two Apple CMF 2026 reference modes — one for P3 color primaries and one that includes both P3 and Adobe RGB color primaries for more flexibility. Peak brightness with both HDR and SDR content is 2,000 nits (on the XDR monitor peak SDR luminance is up to 1,000 nits), and the True Tone setting automatically adjusts HDR tone mapping, brightness, and white point based on ambient lighting. (An option to disable True Tone is in Displays preferences.)
The MacBook doesn’t require using Apple CMF 2026, as there are 14 more reference color modes that use the CIE 1931 color space — it is still the standard, after all — including DICOM for medical imaging (which is cool, but only useful to those in the medical field). The MacBook also supports Apple Pro Display Calibrator, which includes three calibration methods to adjust the reference color modes, or a custom mode, if necessary. There are options for a full calibration or to fine-tune a calibration with the proper measurement gear, or to visually fine-tune the display.
Color science and display technologies have come a long way since 1931, when the CIE 1931 color space was established. Apple’s development of the Apple CMF 2026 and its standardization efforts — the company is currently working with a CIE technical committee on a proposed standard — is an important step to make sure current display technologies look the same to as many people as possible.
Extending support to the new MacBook expands the user base considerably (let’s face it, more people are buying a touchscreen MacBook, even at $2,900, than a $3,300 professional monitor). And more importantly, it gives professionals that can get the most out of it easier, portable access.

title_en: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
title_fa: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
excerpt_en: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
excerpt_fa: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
content_en:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month.
The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems.
Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”
The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.
Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.
The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site.
“Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.”
The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API.
Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves.
“Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said.
Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem.
While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.”
Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting.
“We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said.

title_en: US investigated Chinese spy plot aimed at Nvidia CEO
title_fa: US investigated Chinese spy plot aimed at Nvidia CEO
excerpt_en: A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud company that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, sources have told the New York Times.
excerpt_fa: A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud company that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, sources have told the New York Times.
content_en:
A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times.
The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.
The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.
But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”
In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them. Alice Huang was said to be a top executive for the firm at the time.

title_en: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
title_fa: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
excerpt_en: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
excerpt_fa: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
content_en:
Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together.
Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago, as development costs have surged.
“We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch.
Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream, a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit.
If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.”
While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
“Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said.
The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC.
Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California.
While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif, Snaptrude, and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings.
Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.”

title_en: SuperMe raises $20M for its network of AI expert profiles
title_fa: SuperMe raises $20M for its network of AI expert profiles
excerpt_en: SuperMe is a network of AI profiles built from the knowledge of real-life experts. When you ask a question, the platform determines which experts are best suited to answer and creates a group chat with their AI profiles.
excerpt_fa: SuperMe is a network of AI profiles built from the knowledge of real-life experts. When you ask a question, the platform determines which experts are best suited to answer and creates a group chat with their AI profiles.
content_en:
When people have career or job questions, they usually tap into their network to find experts who’ve faced a similar predicament and can offer answers. Increasingly, that job is falling to AI.
SuperMe is a network of AI profiles built from the knowledge of real-life experts. When you ask a question, the platform determines which experts are best suited to answer and creates a group chat with their AI profiles.
To scale that network on both sides, meaning more users asking questions and more experts supplying knowledge, the startup announced today that it is raising $20 million in funding led by Kirsten Green at Forerunner, with participation from Greylock Partners.
Casey Winters and Ludo Antonov founded the startup in 2024. Both have experience at large consumer companies. Winters held exec roles at Grubhub, Pinterest, and Eventbrite and has advised companies like Airbnb and Canva part-time. Antonov was head of engineering at multiple startups, including Pinterest, Lyft, and Whatnot.
The two got connected when Winters was advising Whatnot. ChatGPT was becoming popular around the same time, and they decided to build a network business using AI.
“There are these hidden networks in Silicon Valley of who the best people are for niche skills. Our idea was: Could we make that network of who the absolute best people are more transparent, and could we take all of the key insights that are locked inside their heads and make them more readily available?” Winters told TechCrunch over a call.
Users can go to the SuperMe website and type their question into the chatbot to start a group of experts. They can also return to a group they have formed or joined and ask follow-up questions.
You can ask a question like, “Analyze my pitch deck. Which parts of the story are the weakest, and which questions should I be most prepared to answer?” and get answers from AI profiles of longtime VCs like Mercedes Bent, Sarah Tavel, and Josh Elman. Users can also go to these people’s profiles and ask questions directly rather than in a group chat.
To collect knowledge from users, SuperMe scans public sources such as LinkedIn, YouTube, Substack, and blogs. It also draws on connected apps such as Google Drive, Notion, Gmail, and meeting notetaking tools like Granola. SuperMe said some of this data will include personal information and trade secrets, but it makes sure that none of it appears in answers.
The network is currently free, but the startup plans to cap the number of questions users can ask, after which they will have to cough up some money. It is also considering how to give experts incentives to add more knowledge.
SuperMe also works with MCP (Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI chatbots connect to outside tools and data), so users can ask questions from within chatbots such as Claude and ChatGPT.
The startup has about 13 employees. It is hiring on the tech side to improve its AI models for conversation and for matching questions to experts, and on the network side for someone to find experts in subject areas the platform doesn’t yet cover.
Forerunner’s Green said that SuperMe is well positioned to build a platform where AI collaborates with humans.
“I think it’s one of the reasons why this is very timely, and it’s good to have something like this establishing itself when we’re relatively early in this journey,” she told TechCrunch over a call. “Because there’s going to be so many lessons that are going to be learned, and they need to be shared so that people can come along in a productive way. I think that the balance here is to build a network so that you do have a true sharing component where there are incentives and benefits for everybody to contribute what they know.”

title_en: ThermoWorks debuts shorter version of its RFX Meat wireless probe for small cuts
title_fa: ThermoWorks debuts shorter version of its RFX Meat wireless probe for small cuts
excerpt_en: The RFX Meat Mini offers nearly identical performance to the full-sized grilling probe.
excerpt_fa: The RFX Meat Mini offers nearly identical performance to the full-sized grilling probe.
content_en:
ThermoWorks debuts shorter version of its RFX Meat wireless probe for small cuts
The RFX Meat Mini offers nearly identical performance to the full-sized grilling probe.
ThermoWorks' RFX Meat probe is an excellent grilling tool. Once you connect it to a Wi-Fi-enabled RFX Gateway, you can monitor food temperatures on your phone from anywhere. And while wireless temperature probes have been around for a while, the RFX line offers ThermoWorks' proven track record for accuracy. That's one essential tool to have in the pocket of your apron.
As good as the RFX Meat is, the 4.7-inch probe is too long for smaller cuts of meat, poultry and fish. With a minimum immersion line of 3.15 inches, the grilling tool wasn't a great option for things like filet mignon or individual portions of salmon. That changes now, thanks to the new RFX Meat Mini. This shorter version offers almost all of the same features as the original RFX Meat, including four internal temperature sensors, an IP69K waterproof rating (so it's dishwasher safe) and the ability to withstand temperatures up to 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit. The Mini still comes with a charging block that's powered by a AAA battery, which ThermoWorks says is good enough for over 175 charges. The best part is the maximum immersion line is 2.6 inches, and the minimum line is just 2.36 inches.
Other than length, the major difference between the RFX Meat and RFX Meat Mini is longevity. The Mini will last up to 48 hours on a charge, while the RFX Meat can go for over 65 hours. 48 hours is plenty for the longest low-and-slow barbecue session you'd undertake at home, and battery life on the Mini isn't likely to be a concern if you're docking it in the charging block when it's not in use. Only commercial cooks are likely to push the limits of the RFX Meat lineup's battery life.
Like the RFX Meat, the Mini's major differentiator amongst the competition is that it operates on a 433MHz radio frequency rather than Bluetooth or Wi-Fi. This is how the probe connects to the RFX Gateway, which in turn syncs up with your home network and the ThermoWorks app. Radio waves are less susceptible to interference from the thick walls of a grill or smoker. The Gateway also accommodates a separate, wired ambient temperature probe. This setup enables more accurate grill readings than you'd get from wireless food probes that have an ambient sensor on the end; those devices have to contend with evaporative cooling during long cooks, which can impact temperature accuracy.
The RFX Meat Mini is available now for $99, the same price as the RFX Meat (when it isn't on sale). ThermWorks is currently offering a 20 percent discount on the Mini when you purchase either the RFX Gateway or the RFX Meat Starter Kit (which includes a Gateway). Due to the Sub-1GHz radio frequency the probe runs on, you'll need a Gateway in order to use the RFX Meat Mini.

title_en: FromSoftware delays The Duskbloods until 2027
title_fa: FromSoftware delays The Duskbloods until 2027
excerpt_en: The studio is taking more time to refine the "rules and balance" of the Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive.
excerpt_fa: The studio is taking more time to refine the "rules and balance" of the Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive.
content_en:
FromSoftware delays The Duskbloods until 2027
The studio is taking more time to refine the "rules and balance."
FromSoftware had long said it would release Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive The Duskbloods this year, but that's no longer the case. The studio has delayed the multiplayer game, which is in the final stages of development, until sometime in 2027.
The studio wrote on X that, during an August network test, it "saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing."
During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing.
— The Duskbloods (@TheDuskbloods) October 29, 2026
FromSoftware revealed the gothic steampunk game in April 2025 during a Switch 2 showcase. Even if The Duskbloods were ready to go at this point, it probably would have made sense to delay the game to 2027 anyway given that Grand Theft Auto 6 and the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time are about to soak up many players' attention for the rest of the year.
This isn't the first time FromSoft has delayed a game for Switch 2. A port of Elden Ring was originally supposed to arrive in 2025, but the studio didn't bring it to the console until this August. It became apparent that FromSoft needed more time to optimize the port after reports emerged of it having performance issues.

content_en:
DoorDash acquires Instacart in $17 billion delivery service merger
The deal combines the two largest grocery delivery platforms in the US.
DoorDash has struck a deal to acquire rival Instacart in a deal valued at $17 billion. The purchase will combine the two biggest grocery delivery services in the US, assuming it isn't stymied by antitrust scrutiny.
DoorDash gained popularity as a restaurant and takeout option, but it does also offer other shopping services, including grocery delivery. The integration of Instacart's network could help further bolster those features. The Instacart acquisition isn't DoorDash's only recent expansion. Earlier this year, the company began testing a drone delivery program.
Multiple advanced reports, including from The Information and The Wall Street Journal, had recently suggested that Instacart was exploring options for a sale. In addition to DoorDash, at some point Uber was also reportedly a potential buyer.
Today's announcement isn't the first time DoorDash had made a pitch for Instacart; it had been in talks that placed Instacart at a higher valuation back in 2021, but those negotiations reportedly ended due to concerns over price and possible antitrust regulation.

title_en: EasySMX S10 Lite review: A Switch 2 fidget toy with a weird removable faceplate
title_fa: EasySMX S10 Lite review: A Switch 2 fidget toy with a weird removable faceplate
excerpt_en: EasySMX is using Elizabeth Holmes levels of pedantry with this faceplate situation.
excerpt_fa: EasySMX is using Elizabeth Holmes levels of pedantry with this faceplate situation.
content_en:
EasySMX S10 Lite review: A Switch 2 fidget toy with a weird removable faceplate
EasySMX is using Elizabeth Holmes levels of pedantry with this faceplate situation.
Of all the Switch 2 controllers I've reviewed in 2026, this is probably the most unexpected pick. EasySMX isn't as well-known as 8BitDo or Turtle Beach, and the S10 Lite is its most pared-down Switch 2 gamepad, regularly listed for $40. The price is exactly what intrigued me about the S10 Lite in the first place, considering most Switch 2 controllers cost around $70, and Nintendo's own Pro Controller is $90. A feature-rich gamepad that can potentially compete with 8BitDo's incredible, $30 Ultimate 2C? I'm here for it.
And then just as swiftly, I'm gone. While the EasySMX S10 Lite has supremely tactile buttons, Hall effect sticks with a soft-hit feel, motion controls and strong haptics, it also has a semi-transparent, magnetically attached faceplate that's so wonky and cheap-feeling that it overshadows the controller's more attractive features. I'm someone who tends to enjoy oddball ideas in my gaming accessories and I can't fully make sense of the S10 Lite faceplate. The way that EasySMX has chosen to market this removable piece of plastic, using misleading verbiage around the availability of custom options, has only poured fuel on the confusion fire.
First, the basics and the good bits. The EasySMX S10 Lite is indeed light and compact, with a creamy plastic finish along the body and an anti-slip diamond texture on the backs of the grips. There are two buttons on the rear of the controller, mappable by pressing and holding a small nearby input marked M. I wish the rear buttons crept up the sides of the grips more, allowing my fingertips to more comfortably hit them, but they're certainly within reach and nice to have. The S10 Lite comes in two colors, ice blue or pastel pink, and while the pink is clearly the cuter option, they're both charming.
There are some fabulous modern features built into the S10 Lite, including precise, anti-drift Hall effect analog sticks that hit the sides of their enclosures silently and super softly. The sound and feel is comparable to Nintendo's proprietary soft-hit action on the Pro Controller, which is a notable feat. That said, the stick click on the S10 Lite is a little too stiff for my liking, and it does make an audible pop when pressed. I'm not personally complaining about the noise, which I find soothing on an ASMR level, but it's notable when the sticks themselves are so darn pillowy otherwise.
The face buttons are tactile microswitches with a wonderfully clicky sound and feel. However, they're also fairly rigid, especially compared with something like the springy mechanical buttons on Razer's Wolverine V3 Pro (my personal favorite gamepad, though it only supports PC and Xbox, and also costs an eye-watering $200. See? I told you the price point was appealing here). The haptics in the S10 Lite are nice and strong, with four intensity settings, and at most they make a slight whining sound rather than grinding.
The bumpers and wide-flared triggers stand out prominently from the chassis, and the triggers have a clicky microswitch action like the face buttons. While I do adore fidget-toy features in my controllers — and the S10 Lite definitely delivers on this point — in-game, I prefer a smooth and sensitive Hall effect pull in the triggers. It's a tradeoff between satisfying sounds and modern comfort that you'll have to consider for yourself.
I like that the home, GameChat and capture buttons are lined up at the bottom of the controller's face, separate from the plus and minus inputs in the center of the pad. This configuration should reduce the number of random, accidental screenshots that you end up taking while trying to quickly open the inventory in Resident Evil Requiem or peep the menu in Hello Kitty Island Adventure, for completely random example.
The S10 Lite has nine-axis motion controls and a Turbo function that allows you to set input macros to a simple button combo. It's also able to wake up the Switch 2 from afar, one of the raddest features a controller can have. The quick-start card that's included in the box is actually helpful in terms of connecting the gamepad to the console. And what's more, there's a built-in toggle on the backside of the pad that lets you swap between Switch and Switch 2 compatibility, or PC, Android and iOS play. In the box, you get the gamepad, a charging cable and the instruction card.
The gamepad, of course, includes the faceplate, attached with four visible, circular magnets and some tension. When I pulled my S10 Lite out of the box, the bottom ridge of the faceplate wasn't fully tucked into place, raised in a way that was mildly infuriating but not clearly unintentional. It wasn't until I was fidgeting with the controller, waiting for a game to download, that I realized I could pop in the transparent-blue plastic so it sat flat along the bottom. Even still, the left side of my faceplate refuses to depress as deeply as the right, so there's a sliver of icy plastic peering over one grip, catching my fingertips and compelling me to pick at it. I may be able to adjust this by tightening a tiny screw on that side, but all things considered, I'd rather not have to.
This leads us to the obvious question: Why have a removable faceplate in the first place? It would make sense if EasySMX had, say, a marketplace of cute alternatives that anyone could purchase and swap into their own pad, allowing the brand to jump on trends and collaborate with cool creators, naturally extending the money-making potential of the S10 Lite. That would make perfect sense. But that's not what EasySMX is doing.
The controller's product page provides just one sentence about faceplates, reading, "DIY Your Controller: express your personality with DIY Magnetic Faceplates & Stickers, allowing you to swap covers instantly to match your mood or your favorite game theme." Those first...

title_en: Apple and Google fined in South Korea over app store violations
title_fa: Apple and Google fined in South Korea over app store violations
excerpt_en: South Korean regulators found that Apple and Google violated the country's Telecommunications Business Act.
excerpt_fa: South Korean regulators found that Apple and Google violated the country's Telecommunications Business Act.
content_en:
Apple and Google fined in South Korea over app store violations
Regulators are also requiring them to change their business practices.
Both Apple and Google have violated Korea's Telecommunications Business Act, the country's communications regulator has determined. The companies have received penalties from the regulator and have been ordered to change their business practices related to their app stores. Google was slapped with a KRW 42.9 billion ($32 million) fine, while Apple has to pay KRW 20.81 billion ($15.6 million) in penalties.
According to the Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC), it has conducted fact-finding investigations and on-site inspections on the companies since 2022. The agency found that the two of them violated the country's rules for the app market sector, including forcing people to use their in-app payment methods, imposing a commission of 26 percent for third-party payments and prohibiting external payments.
It also said that the company delayed app reviews without providing a clear reason for it and didn't responding to individual inquiries about the delays. Finally, the regulator found that Apple computed its commissions differently for South Korean and overseas developers. For Korean developers, it based its cut on the price of purchases including VAT, while it based its cut on pre-VAT prices for developers from outside the country.
As a result of those findings, the KMCC is requiring the companies to accept external payments and to revise their app review procedures. Apple is also required to prevent "discrimination between domestic and overseas app developers." The companies already allow external payments in the US and in the European Union.

title_en: Hackers leaked details of more than 41,000 Homeland Security personnel
title_fa: Hackers leaked details of more than 41,000 Homeland Security personnel
excerpt_en: A hacktivist group stole the information of ICE agents and border police from Homeland Security.
excerpt_fa: A hacktivist group stole the information of ICE agents and border police from Homeland Security.
content_en:
Hackers leaked details of more than 41,000 Homeland Security personnel
They include email addresses and phone numbers of ICE agents and border police.
A hacktivist group stole records for more than 41,000 Homeland Security personnel and got help to release it on the web, according to Wired, the Washington Post and NPR. The leaked records contain email addresses, phone numbers and office addresses of the personnel, but they also include sensitive information about the agency's undercover and surveillance programs.
Of the records that were leaked, 21,000 identify people working with the US Customs and Border Protection, while 10,000 records belong to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel. A third of those records is related to the Homeland Security Investigations unit, the criminal investigative arm of ICE. Overall, the leaks expose the details of a seventh of Homeland Security's workforce.
"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace said in a statement. They're talking about the DHS' Secretary's words during a press conference, wherein he said that the agency is "turning up the heat on the streets" when asked how it would hold the agents who violated its use of force policy accountable. The agency held the press conference following the fatal shootings of Joan Sebastian Duran Guerrero from Maine and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo from Houston, neither of whom were subject to ICE's enforcement activities.
The group apparently stole the data via Okta, the single sign-on service used by the DHS. With Okta, users just have to sign on once with their credentials to get full access to a system's backend, cloud service and/or mobile apps. Okta told Wired that it has found no evidence that its "data or systems were compromised." The hackers shared the data with transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and a Swiss cybersecurity researcher called maia arson crimew. They created a searchable online database using the information the Department of Peace had provided.
"They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," the hackers wrote in a note with the stolen records. The Distributed Denial of Secrets is calling the database "Icepick." Its founder, Emma Best, said the records contain links between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations ...along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."
Meanwhile, a Homeland Security spokesperson said it is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." They added: "We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available."

title_en: Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
title_fa: Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
excerpt_en: On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a "long-term goal" of pushing the computer industry to create "a fully domestic supply...
excerpt_fa: On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a "long-term goal" of pushing the computer industry to create "a fully domestic supply...
content_en:
On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a “long-term goal” of pushing the computer industry to create “a fully domestic supply chain.”
Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
Palmer Luckey says it was always the goal, and now the company is committing to it.
Palmer Luckey says it was always the goal, and now the company is committing to it.
Even a single Made-in-USA laptop would be a surprise, because no major US computer company builds its laptops here — not Apple, not Dell, not HP, not Microsoft. We’re not aware of any company that does.
But we are aware of companies that have briefly and strategically assembled computers here seemingly to appease President Donald Trump. We’re also aware of companies that have promised US jobs only to deliver empty buildings. And we’re aware of at least one fake “US” company that lied to the government about making product domestically.
That’s why we now ask pointed questions when a company says it’s committed to US manufacturing. We asked TP-Link those sorts of questions just over a week ago. On Monday, we asked Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Qualcomm president and CEO Cristiano Amon those kinds of questions.
Over the course of two days, Anduril has changed one important answer.
Anduril communications VP Shannon Prior now says the company’s laptop will have at least 65 percent of its components made in the US by the time it launches in 2027. It’s an important number, and one that Anduril did not commit to earlier this week.
Luckey held a call with reporters on Monday, during which he was clear that he wants to make literally every part of a computer in the United States — and that Anduril and Qualcomm have already mapped out a plan. “We have a technical roadmap to get to 100 percent domestic over time,” he told journalists.
Luckey also suggested his laptop would be built to comply with the requirements of the military and other government agencies — and that it would meet or exceed one specific US government standard that has an exact definition.
“We are not just barely meeting the bar for Made in America. We are going hard to make this an all-American play, and not even the Buy American Act requires what we’re trying,” Luckey said.
The Buy American Act dates back to 1933, but it was updated during the Biden Administration to require that at least 65 percent of the cost of a product’s components must be made domestically for it be considered a domestic product itself. That number is going up to 75 percent in 2029.
Many products need to be made in America to those standards, or federal agencies can’t buy them without receiving a waiver — which agencies currently use en masse, Luckey himself argued on the call. “There’s a number of government agencies that are required by law to buy American-made computers [...] All of those procurements are happening under waivers of those laws,” he said.
We also noticed that Anduril’s press release specifies that its first laptop will be “designed and assembled” in the United States, not necessarily “manufactured” here (though the release does talk about future manufacturing). This was also a sticking point with router maker TP-Link, which would not confirm full manufacturing even after suggesting it in an interview with The Verge.
That’s why we asked Luckey what percent of his first laptop’s components would be made in the US. His reply was not 65 percent or 70 percent. It was “TBD.” You can read the exchange for yourself:
The Verge: When it arrives in 2027, what percent of the components in the BlueChip laptop will be made in the US?
Luckey: TBD. I’m doing my very, very best. It’s gonna be a whole mix of things based on when do certain memory fabs come online? When do certain CPU, GPU fabs come online? There’s a whole— Like, am I able to get a display line here or not? Do I have to do that after launch? I’m being totally open kimono with you here. Those questions are not settled. It is not clear if I will be able. I know the glass is gonna be made in the US, I know the frame is gonna be made in the US around that display. I know that parts of the ribbon component are gonna be made in the U.S. I don’t know if I will have successfully pulled that component in or a dozen other components. So it’s a little up in the air. I’m doing my very, very best. I think most likely the thing that we ship is not going to be 100-percent American. I think it’ll be a blend of US and allies around the world, mostly US, probably a few things from some allies, and then that’ll be in the context of conversations with those allies about bringing those components into production in the United States, and I’m being honest with the government on this too. I mean, I’ve had conversations where I’ve said, listen. I would love to give you guys an American, 100-percent American laptop right off the bat, but that is not the environment the US government has created or US industry has created. I can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.
When we followed up by email to ask specifically about 65 percent, the answer was that the laptop prototype is currently at 32 percent and Anduril could not yet commit to 65 percent. Here’s Anduril spokesperson Stephanie Davis’ full reply on Tuesday:
For the prototype today, approximately 32% is U.S.-origin by component procurement cost, and more than 90% is sourced from the United States and allied countries combined.
We’re working to expand domestic sourcing and production ahead of planned availability in 2027, with the goal of eliminating foreign content and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain.
The final domestic-content percentage at launch remains unsettled, so we can’t confirm above or below 65% today. That’s why we’re asking you to revise the assertion that it will be “well below” that...
